contribution: The course's main debate: students argue the motion that governments should invest more public money in fusion research, with nine dated evidence cards on both sides, defined roles and timing, debate language, a rebuttal exercise and transparent assessment criteria.
learn: argue for or against public money for fusion with claim, evidence and reasoning.
evaluate the strength of evidence and rebut the strongest argument of the other side.
use polite English debate language to state, concede, question and sum up.
prior: Established results, institutional plans and corporate claims are different kinds of statements (chapter *Fusion in the energy system*)
The fusion gain $Q$ compares fusion power with heating power, not with electricity (chapter *Inside ITER: the machine and fusion gain*)

activities.text: Imagine that your country's parliament is planning next year's research budget. One member wants to double the money for fusion research: "It is the energy source of the future." Another wants to move the money to solar power and batteries: "We need solutions now, not in 2050." Both are well informed. Today you will take part in their debate.
activities.question: Should governments invest more public money in fusion research, and how can you decide?

activities.title: Review: what kind of statement?
activities.prompt: In the chapter *Fusion in the energy system*, you sorted statements into established results, institutional plans and corporate claims. Which of these is an **institutional plan**?

choices.text: ITER's 2024 baseline sets deuterium–tritium operation for 2039.
choices.feedback: Right. An intergovernmental organisation's schedule is a plan: it says what it intends, and it can change, as ITER's schedule has before.

choices.text: JET released $69\ \text{MJ}$ of fusion heat in one pulse in 2023.
choices.feedback: This has already happened and was measured: an established result. A plan is about the future.

choices.text: A company says it will sell fusion electricity from 2028.
choices.feedback: This is about the future, but it comes from a private company, so it is a corporate claim, not an institutional plan.

choices.text: Tritium decays with a half-life of $12.3$ years.
choices.feedback: A measured property of nature: an established result, not a plan.

activities.text:
Sentence starters

  • At the moment, I am for / against / undecided, because …
  • I think public money should go to …
  • What worries me most is …
  • I would change my mind if …

activities.title: Think about it: your first opinion
activities.pair: Pair work: tell your partner your first opinion in one minute, then each of you writes it down. Keep it: you will compare it with your opinion after the debate.
activities.prompt: Discuss with a partner, then write two or three sentences. Are you for, against or undecided about the motion *"Governments should invest more public money in fusion research"*? Give one reason, and say what kind of evidence could change your mind.
activities.model: At the moment, I am undecided. I think fusion could give clean energy in the future, but what worries me most is that it has taken so long and cost so much. I would change my mind if I saw evidence that fusion can produce electricity at a reasonable price, or that other energy sources need the money more.
criteria: The answer takes a clear position (for, against or undecided).
The answer gives at least one reason.
The answer names a kind of evidence that could change the writer's mind.

activities.title: Prediction 1: whose money?
activities.prompt: By July 2026, private fusion companies had raised USD 14.24 billion in total. About how much of this came from **public** sources (governments and public agencies)?

choices.text: About USD 1 billion, under a tenth
choices.feedback: Right. Card E: about USD 0.98 billion of USD 14.24 billion, about $7\ \%$. The rest came from private investors. Both teams can use this: investors pay most of the bill, but the companies still ask for government support.

choices.text: About USD 7 billion, about half
choices.feedback: Card E gives much less: about USD 0.98 billion, about $7\ \%$ of the total. Most of the money of fusion companies comes from private investors.

choices.text: About USD 13 billion, almost all
choices.feedback: The opposite: private investors gave about USD 13.26 billion and public sources only about USD 0.98 billion (card E). Public money for fusion goes mainly to public laboratories and to ITER, not to companies.

choices.text: Nothing: companies use only private money
choices.feedback: Card E shows about USD 0.98 billion of public money, about $7\ \%$. Governments also give companies milestone-based grants, as card I shows for Commonwealth Fusion Systems.

activities.title: Prediction 2: where do companies come from?
activities.prompt: Commonwealth Fusion Systems is one of the best-funded fusion companies; it builds the SPARC tokamak in Massachusetts. Where did the company come from?

choices.text: A spin-off of a university laboratory
choices.feedback: Right. Card I: it was founded in 2018 as a spin-off from MIT's Plasma Science and Fusion Center, where the Alcator C-Mod tokamak had run for 25 years with US government money. The proposition will use this: public research created the company.

choices.text: The research department of an oil company
choices.feedback: An oil company (Eni) was an early investor, but the company itself came from a university: it is a 2018 spin-off of MIT's Plasma Science and Fusion Center (card I).

choices.text: A former nuclear weapons laboratory
choices.feedback: Some fusion research is done at weapons laboratories, such as NIF, but this company is a 2018 spin-off of MIT's Plasma Science and Fusion Center (card I).

choices.text: A start-up of investors with no laboratory
choices.feedback: Investors pay for it today, but its knowledge came from a university laboratory: it began in 2018 as a spin-off of MIT's Plasma Science and Fusion Center (card I).

activities.title: Sort the evidence
activities.text: Decide which side each card supports best. You will defend your choices in the debate.

Word bank

evidence · source · reliable · result · plan · claim · cost · delay · investment · public money · private investment · to support · to weaken · to outweigh

Sentence starters

  • The strongest card for the proposition is …, because …
  • The strongest card for the opposition is …, because …
  • Card … is weaker, because it is only a plan / a claim.
  • Card … could help both sides: …

activities.title: Discuss: the strongest card for each side
activities.pair: Group work in fours: two of you look for the proposition's best card, two for the opposition's; then compare.
activities.prompt: Discuss in your group, then write four sentences. Which card is the strongest for each side, and why? Which card is the weakest, and why? Use the words *result*, *plan* or *claim* at least once.
activities.model: The strongest card for the proposition is card A, because it reports measured results: JET's $69\ \text{MJ}$ in 2023 and NIF's $3.15\ \text{MJ}$ in 2022 show that the science is improving. The strongest card for the opposition is card F, because ITER's construction estimate of $5.9$ billion euros (2006) has become $18\text{–}22$ billion euros for construction and operation, and its schedule has slipped; this is a documented history of official estimates, not a company's guess. Card H is weaker for both sides as evidence about fusion itself, because STEP's 2040 date is only a plan. Card E could help both sides: investors believe in fusion, but that may mean the state does not need to pay.
criteria: The answer names one card for each side and gives a reason based on what the card shows.
The answer judges the strength of the evidence (result, plan or claim; the source).
The answer names a weaker card and explains why it is weaker.
The answer uses at least two words from the word bank.

activities.title: Optional source: nuclear energy and climate (video)
activities.prompt: Watch the video below (9 minutes) at home or with headphones. It is about **fission**, not fusion. Then write three or four sentences: Who made the video, and when? Which one argument from it could a team use in today's debate, and for which side? What are the limits of this source for a debate about fusion? You can start with *The video was made by … in …*, *One argument we could use is …* and *A limit of this source is …*.
activities.model: The video was made by Kurzgesagt – In a Nutshell, a popular-science channel, and published on 13 April 2021. Its question is whether we need nuclear energy to stop climate change, and its description says the answer is "complicated". A team could use its point that low-carbon power that runs whatever the weather is valuable; the proposition could say that fusion might one day give the same benefit without long-lived waste. The limits are that it is about fission, not fusion, that it is from 2021, and that an animated video is a summary, so the team should check its numbers in the sources it lists.
criteria: The answer names the creator and the date of the video.
The answer takes one argument from the video and connects it to fusion and to one side of the motion.
The answer names at least one limit of the source (topic is fission, date, type of source).

activities.title: Debate language
activities.text:
Learn the phrases that do the work in a debate.

Sentence starters for every speech

  • Chair: Welcome to the debate. I now give the floor to … · You have 30 seconds left. · Thank you; time is up.
  • Opening: Madam / Mr Chair, we believe that … Our first argument is … Our second argument is …
  • Evidence: According to … (date), … · The figures on card … show that …
  • Rebuttal: Our opponents claim that …, but … · This argument ignores the fact that …
  • Conceding: We accept that …; however, … · That is a fair point, but …
  • Question: Could you explain how …? · Where does that number come from?
  • Closing: To sum up, … · The strongest reason is … · For these reasons, we urge you to vote for / against the motion.

activities.title: Back to your predictions
activities.prompt: Compare your predictions with cards E and I. Which fact surprised you more, and which team will it help? You can start with *I expected …, but card … shows …*.

activities.text:
Your teacher gives each student a role: proposition, opposition, chair, fact-checker or judge (see the table above). Teams have 12 minutes to prepare. Plan three arguments with claim, evidence and reasoning, decide who speaks when, and predict the other side's strongest argument so that you can rebut it. Rebuttal speakers write two lines of the form *Our opponents will say …, but …*; closing speakers choose the one card they will repeat at the end. The chair learns the chair's phrases below. Fact-checkers prepare by noting the key numbers and dates of every card; judges read the four criteria.

Sentence starters

  • We believe that … Our first argument is that …
  • According to card …, … This shows that …
  • Our opponents will probably say that …, but …
  • We accept that …; however, …

activities.title: Write your team's opening speech
activities.pair: Team work: plan together, then each speaker writes their own part; the first speaker reads the opening speech in the debate.
activities.prompt: Write the opening speech of your team (about 100–150 words, about 2 minutes when spoken). State your position, give two arguments, each with a card (source and date) and your reasoning, and end with one sentence that the listeners will remember. Fact-checkers and judges: write the opening speech of the side you find *less* convincing.
activities.model:
Proposition: Madam Chair, we believe that governments should invest more public money in fusion research. Our first argument is that the science is working. According to EUROfusion, JET released $69\ \text{MJ}$ of fusion heat in one pulse in 2023, and in 2022 the National Ignition Facility released more energy than its laser light delivered. These are measured results, not promises. Our second argument is that public research builds industries: Commonwealth Fusion Systems began in 2018 as a spin-off of a publicly funded MIT laboratory, and companies themselves still ask for government support. We accept that ITER is over budget; however, every first-of-a-kind machine is. Fusion fuel would last for centuries. Let us not stop halfway to a new source of energy.

Opposition (alternative model): Madam Chair, we believe that governments should not invest more public money in fusion. Our first argument is cost and delay. ITER's construction was estimated at $5.9$ billion euros in 2006; later estimates of construction and operation are $18\text{–}22$ billion euros, and its deuterium–tritium experiments are planned only from 2039. Our second argument is that fusion has not yet made any electricity: NIF's lasers used about $300\ \text{MJ}$ of electricity for one shot, and ITER will produce none. Meanwhile, the IPCC says emissions must fall by about $45\ \%$ by 2030, and renewables already gave $33.8\ \%$ of the world's electricity in 2025. We accept that fusion research is exciting; however, public money should go where it cuts emissions soonest.
criteria: The speech states the team's position on the motion clearly at the start.
The speech gives two arguments, each with a card's fact, its source and its date.
Each argument explains *why* the fact supports the position (reasoning).
The speech keeps results, plans and claims apart and never presents gain as electricity.
The speech ends with a short, memorable sentence and stays within about 150 words.

activities.title: Choose the best rebuttal
activities.prompt: The opposition says: *"ITER's cost has tripled. Fusion is a waste of public money."* Which reply by the proposition is the best rebuttal?

choices.text: "We accept the cost grew; however, records keep improving."
choices.feedback: Right. It concedes a true point, then answers with evidence (results such as card A) and reasoning. Conceding makes the speaker more credible.

choices.text: "Our opponents clearly do not understand physics at all."
choices.feedback: This attacks the speakers, not the argument, and gives no evidence. Judges score it low on reasoning and language.

choices.text: "ITER will give ten times more energy, so it pays back the cost."
choices.feedback: This mixes up gain and electricity: $Q = 10$ compares fusion power with heating power, and ITER will produce no electricity (card G).

choices.text: "Fusion powers the Sun, so it will surely work on Earth."
choices.feedback: The Sun shows that fusion is possible, but not that a power plant on Earth will be affordable. It does not answer the argument about cost.

activities.title: Run the debate
activities.text:
Follow the order and the time limits in *How a structured debate works*. The chair keeps time and gives the floor. While the teams speak:

- **Fact-checkers** write down every number and date a speaker uses and compare it with the cards. In their report they say which facts were correct and correct any mistakes politely: *"The speaker said …; card … says …."*
- **Judges** give each team 0–3 points for evidence, accuracy, reasoning and language, and note one strong argument from each side.
- **Everyone** votes twice, before the opening speeches and after the closing speeches. The team that changes more votes wins.

activities.title: 1. Concept: the weakest argument
activities.prompt: Which of these arguments is the weakest, because it has no evidence that supports its claim?

choices.text: "Everyone knows fusion is the future, so we should pay for it."
choices.feedback: Right. *Everyone knows* is not evidence: it gives no source, no date and no reasoning. The other three each rest on a checkable fact.

choices.text: "JET released $69\ \text{MJ}$ in 2023, so the science is advancing."
choices.feedback: This uses a measured result with a date (card A) and draws a modest conclusion from it. It is not the weakest.

choices.text: "ITER's cost rose from $5.9$ to $18\text{–}22$ billion euros, a warning sign."
choices.feedback: This uses a documented fact (card F) and gives a reason. Whether it is a *warning* is debatable, but it is evidence-based.

choices.text: "Renewables gave $33.8\ \%$ of electricity in 2025, so they work now."
choices.feedback: This uses an official statistic with its year (card D). It is an evidence-based argument, even if the other side disagrees with the conclusion.

activities.title: 2. Fact-check a speaker
activities.prompt: A speaker says: *"In 2022 the National Ignition Facility proved that fusion produces more energy than it uses."* What should the fact-checker say?

choices.text: Correct: NIF released more energy than its whole facility used.
choices.feedback: No: the whole facility used far more. The lasers alone drew about $300\ \text{MJ}$ of electricity to make $2.05\ \text{MJ}$ of light (card G).

choices.text: Partly wrong: it beat the laser light, not the electricity used.
choices.feedback: Right. NIF released $3.15\ \text{MJ}$ from $2.05\ \text{MJ}$ of laser light on the target, but the lasers drew about $300\ \text{MJ}$ from the grid (cards A and G).

choices.text: Wrong: NIF has never released more energy than it received.
choices.feedback: It has: on 5 December 2022 it released $3.15\ \text{MJ}$ from $2.05\ \text{MJ}$ of laser light (card A). The speaker's mistake is about *which* energy was exceeded.

choices.text: Wrong: the result came from JET in the UK, not from NIF.
choices.feedback: The source is right: NIF in California. JET's record (card A) was a different experiment, a tokamak pulse of $69\ \text{MJ}$ in 2023.

activities.title: 3. Evidence and reasoning
activities.prompt: Both teams use card E (private money). Which sentence adds **reasoning** to the evidence, instead of only repeating it?

choices.text: "Firms raised USD 4.48 billion in a year, as card E says."
choices.feedback: This only repeats the fact. Reasoning explains what the fact means for the motion.

choices.text: "Investors gave billions, so the state can fund other needs."
choices.feedback: Right. It links the evidence to a conclusion about public money: if private investors pay, the state's money can go elsewhere. The other team may disagree, but this is an argument.

choices.text: "Card E comes from the Fusion Industry Association in 2026."
choices.feedback: Naming the source and date is good practice, but it is not reasoning: it does not say what the fact shows.

choices.text: "There were 56 fusion companies in the survey of 2026."
choices.feedback: Another fact from the card, without a link to the motion. Reasoning answers the question *so what?*

activities.text:
Sentence starters

  • Before the debate I was …; now I am …, because …
  • The most convincing argument was …, because …
  • I accept that …; however, …
  • On balance, I believe that governments should / should not …

activities.title: 4. Write: your position after the debate
activities.prompt: Write a paragraph of 120–150 words in your own name (not your debate role). Is your opinion now for, against or undecided? Compare it with your first opinion. Give your main argument with one card (source and date) and your reasoning, and answer the strongest argument of the other side.
activities.model: Before the debate I was undecided; now I am, on balance, for more public money, but only for research with clear milestones. The most convincing argument was that public research created the knowledge that companies now use: Commonwealth Fusion Systems began in 2018 as a spin-off of a publicly funded MIT laboratory (card I). Without that money, the private investment of USD 4.48 billion in 2025–2026 (card E) would probably not exist. I accept that ITER's estimates have grown to $18\text{–}22$ billion euros and that no fusion device has yet made electricity (cards F and G); however, this is a reason to fund research carefully, not to stop it. Because fusion is not planned to deliver electricity before 2030 and the public prototype STEP targets 2040, I think most climate money should still go to renewables and grids, and fusion should get a smaller, long-term share.
criteria: The answer states a clear position and compares it with the first opinion.
The main argument uses at least one card with its source or date.
The reasoning links the evidence to the question of *public* money.
The answer names and answers the strongest argument of the other side (rebuttal or concession).
The answer keeps results, plans and claims apart and uses debate language (*I accept that …; however, …*).

activities.text:
Le coin français

French debates also use these phrases: à mon avis, je suis d'accord, je ne suis pas d'accord. Listen, repeat, and then give your opinion on l'argent public pour la recherche sur la fusion in one French sentence to your partner. In the hints, capitals show the stressed syllable, and õ, ã are nasal vowels: the air goes through the nose and no n is heard.
